grammarGuide.title: Tense & aspect · 시제와 상
grammarGuide.summary: Korean tense is carried mainly by the predicate, while aspect shows whether an action is ongoing, completed, repeated, or in a resulting state.

items.label: Present / general
items.example: 한국어를 공부해요. — I study Korean / I am studying Korean.

items.label: Past
items.example: 어제 공부했어요. — I studied yesterday.

items.label: Future / plan
items.example: 내일 공부할 거예요. — I will study tomorrow.

items.label: Progressive
items.example: 지금 공부하고 있어요. — I am studying now.

items.label: Resulting state
items.example: 문이 열려 있어요. — The door is open / remains opened.

items.label: Experience / completion
items.example: 김치를 먹어 봤어요. — I have tried kimchi.

grammarGuide.note: Do not force every Korean ending into one English tense label. Korean endings also express intention, evidence, politeness, and the speaker’s attitude.

grammarGuide.title: Negation · 부정
grammarGuide.summary: Korean distinguishes ordinary negation from inability, and often offers both a short and a long form.

items.label: Not · short
items.example: 오늘 학교에 안 가요. — I am not going to school today.

items.label: Not · long
items.example: 커피를 마시지 않아요. — I do not drink coffee.

items.label: Cannot · short
items.example: 오늘 운동을 못 해요. — I cannot exercise today.

items.label: Cannot · long
items.example: 어제 잠을 자지 못했어요. — I could not sleep yesterday.

grammarGuide.note: 안 usually means ‘do not / choose not to’; 못 usually points to inability or circumstances preventing the action.

grammarGuide.title: Passive & causative · 피동과 사동
grammarGuide.summary: Korean does not have one universal passive or causative ending. It uses lexical suffixes, productive constructions, and noun-based patterns.

items.label: Lexical passive
items.example: 문이 닫혔어요. — The door was closed. / 이름이 불렸어요. — The name was called.

items.label: Productive passive / change
items.example: 이 노래가 많이 알려졌어요. — This song became widely known.

items.label: Noun + passive/result
items.example: 계획이 결정됐어요. — The plan was decided.

items.label: Lexical causative
items.example: 아이에게 밥을 먹였어요. — I fed the child / made the child eat.

items.label: Productive causative
items.example: 학생들이 말하게 했어요. — I made / let the students speak.

items.label: Action noun causative
items.example: 학생들을 공부시켰어요. — I made the students study.

grammarGuide.note: Many passive and causative forms are lexical: the exact suffix is tied to the verb. Learn common pairs as vocabulary rather than trying to guess mechanically. -게 하다 is much more productive and can mean ‘make’ or ‘let’ depending on context.

grammarGuide.title: Connecting ideas · 연결어미
grammarGuide.summary: Connectors show sequence, contrast, reason, condition, concession, and purpose. Learn the relationship between clauses rather than translating one English conjunction at a time.

items.label: And / sequence
items.example: 밥을 먹고 공부해요. — I eat and then study.

items.label: Reason / sequence
items.example: 비가 와서 집에 있었어요. — It rained, so I stayed home.

items.label: Reason / speaker judgment
items.example: 늦었으니까 빨리 가요. — We are late, so let’s hurry.

items.label: Because of noun
items.example: 시험 때문에 바빠요. — I am busy because of the test.

items.label: If / when
items.example: 시간이 있으면 같이 가요. — If you have time, let’s go together.

items.label: Although / but
items.example: 비싸지만 좋아요. — It is expensive, but I like it.

wordBuilding.title: Noun + 하다 → action or descriptive predicate
wordBuilding.summary: One of the most productive Korean patterns. Many Sino-Korean nouns combine with 하다 and behave as verbs or descriptive verbs.

patterns.meaning: necessity + do → to be necessary / need

wordBuilding.note: Not every noun can freely take 하다. Treat established combinations as lexical items even though the pattern is highly productive.

wordBuilding.title: Noun + 되다 / 시키다
wordBuilding.summary: With many action nouns, 되다 often gives a passive/result meaning, while 시키다 gives a causative meaning.

patterns.meaning: prepare → make someone prepare / get something prepared

wordBuilding.note: 하다 / 되다 / 시키다 often form useful families, especially with Sino-Korean vocabulary.

wordBuilding.title: High-value Sino-Korean suffixes
wordBuilding.summary: Recognizing common suffixes lets you infer families of words instead of memorizing every item independently.

patterns.meaning: forms ‘-al / -ic’ ideas: 문화적 cultural, 개인적 personal
property / possibility: 가능성 possibility, 중요성 importance
person associated with an action/role: 사용자 user, 참가자 participant
member / worker: 회사원 office worker, 점원 store clerk

wordBuilding.note: These are especially helpful for Chinese readers because the Hanja often makes the semantic relationship visible immediately.

native.title: Native Korean numbers · 고유어 수
native.summary: Common for hours, age, and many counters.

sino.title: Sino-Korean numbers · 한자어 수
sino.summary: Common for dates, money, phone numbers, minutes, measurements, floors, and larger calculations.

compare.why: age with 살 usually uses Native Korean
counter 권 takes Native Korean numerals

speechLevels.name: 해체 · casual non-polite
speechLevels.use: Close friends, younger family members, children, or people who have mutually agreed to use 반말.
speechLevels.warning: Do not default to this with strangers, teachers, or older people just because the grammar is easier.

speechLevels.name: 해요체 · everyday polite
speechLevels.use: The safest default for many everyday conversations with adults you are not extremely close to.
speechLevels.warning: Polite does not automatically mean honorific: subject honorific -(으)시- is a separate choice.

speechLevels.name: 하십시오체 · formal polite
speechLevels.use: Announcements, presentations, military/service contexts, formal interviews, customer-facing situations, and highly formal speech.
speechLevels.warning: The declarative -ㅂ니다/습니다 and question -ㅂ니까/습니까 forms differ.

speechLevels.name: 해라체 / plain style · formal non-polite
speechLevels.use: Writing, diaries, reports, narration, quotations of general facts, and some hierarchical speech. Very common in written Korean even though it is not a normal polite conversation style.
speechLevels.warning: Calling it simply ‘rude’ is misleading: in writing it often functions as a neutral plain style.

honorificSystem.label: Humble speaker verb
honorificSystem.meaning: lowers the speaker’s action relative to the respected person

culture.title: 김치 · Kimchi
culture.summary: A broad family of fermented vegetable dishes. Napa-cabbage kimchi is famous, but there are many regional and seasonal varieties.
culture.language: 김치 is commonly served as 반찬, a side dish shared with a meal.

culture.title: 비빔밥 · Bibimbap
culture.summary: Rice mixed with vegetables and other toppings, often with gochujang.
culture.language: 비비다 means to mix; 밥 means cooked rice / meal.

culture.title: 불고기 · Bulgogi
culture.summary: Thinly sliced marinated meat, usually beef, cooked by grilling or pan-cooking.
culture.language: 불 means fire and 고기 means meat.

culture.title: 떡볶이 · Tteokbokki
culture.summary: A popular snack built around chewy rice cakes, commonly served in a spicy-sweet sauce.
culture.language: 떡 rice cake · 볶다 to stir-fry.

culture.title: 김밥 · Gimbap
culture.summary: Rice and assorted fillings rolled in dried seaweed and sliced into pieces.

culture.title: 미역국 · Seaweed soup
culture.summary: A seaweed soup especially associated with birthdays in Korea and also eaten in everyday meals.
culture.language: 생일 birthday · 미역 seaweed · 국 soup.

culture.title: 반찬 and shared dishes
culture.summary: Korean meals often include several side dishes placed in the center of the table.
culture.language: 반찬 means side dish; 같이 먹어요 means ‘let’s eat together.’

culture.title: Names, titles, and respect
culture.summary: Using a person’s name, title, kinship term, or 씨 depends on relationship and context. Korean often avoids repeatedly using ‘you’ where English would use it.
culture.language: 선생님, 교수님, 사장님 and family-style terms can function as forms of address.

culture.title: 설날 and 추석
culture.summary: 설날 is Lunar New Year and 추석 is a major harvest holiday. Traditions vary by household.
culture.language: 새해 복 많이 받으세요 is a common New Year greeting.

culture.title: 전화 etiquette
culture.summary: Telephone Korean uses conventional expressions such as 여보세요 and polite requests for asking to speak to someone.
culture.language: 여보세요 → 누구세요? → ___ 씨 좀 바꿔 주세요 → 안녕히 계세요 / 끊을게요.
